title: Memorizing chains
hookLine: students memorized chains and texts by heart

lines: KEPT WHERE NO THIEF COULD REACH.
cards: So-and-so told us, from so-and-so, from so-and-so, who heard the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ say. That's how the lesson begins, in a circle of students on a mosque floor, with no book open. Names first, then the saying.

The students hold the names too, in order, because the names are how anyone will later know whether the saying can be trusted. Drop one link and the report limps. Swap two names and a careful critic will notice.
Tradition tells of students who kept both, chain and text, in the one place no thief could reach. Today: memorizing chains.

teach.b: Start with the little word that did the heavy lifting: haddathana, he told us. In the collections it comes link after link, and each one is a person who sat in front of another person.
To memorize a chain was to memorize a line of people.

teach.h: MEMORY AND PAPER CHECK EACH OTHER.
teach.b: Next, why memory, when there was paper? Scholars wrote as well, and their notebooks mattered. But the two checked each other.
A student who knew a report by heart could catch a copyist's slip, and a written page could catch a slip of memory. Then the reason underneath it all.
In a report preserved by al-Tirmidhi, the Prophet asks Allah to make radiant the face of a person who hears a saying from him, holds on to it, and passes it on.
In another version, the person passes it on just as he heard it. That phrase sits under the whole enterprise, and it's why a narrator's memory was tested alongside his honesty.

Last, a look back, because today closes the week. The four books of the Shia. The sacred hadith, where Allah speaks in the Prophet's phrasing: I am as My servant thinks of Me; whoever comes walking, He comes running.
Islam, iman and ihsan, taught in one scene. Women like Karimah, who taught the Sahih.

teach.h: A WEEK OF THINGS HELD BY HEART.
teach.b: Every one of those reached this lesson because a person held it carefully, often by heart, and handed it on just as it was heard.

how: Students of hadith traditionally learn reports with their chains from a teacher, and many Muslims memorize short hadith, such as "religion is sincere counsel", as a way of keeping them close.

the chain was held together with the text, because the names are how a report is tested.

games.q: you're a student. your teacher has recited a report, and you realize you've lost one name in the middle of the chain. what do you do?
o: fill in the name that seems most likely.
go back, ask, and pass it on just as you heard it.
pass on the saying with no chain at all.
games.why: the whole craft leans on passing it on just as you heard it. a guessed name is exactly what a critic would catch.

practice: Here's a short hadith from Sahih Muslim, in plain English: religion is sincere counsel.
Say it slowly, then again with your eyes closed, then give it a simple chain, Muslim, from those before him, from Tamim al-Dari, from the Prophet, and say the chain before the line.
If you pray, you can carry the line into your prayer; if not, just sit with those four words.

wordCard.voice: Memorizing chains. Holding the names of the narrators, in order, together with the words they carried, by heart. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: guarding, keeping safe, and so learning by heart.
